𑌶𑍍𑌰𑍀𑌮𑌧𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌜𑍁𑌨𑌭𑌾𑌲𑌚𑌨𑍍𑌦𑍍𑌰𑌮𑌖𑌿𑌰𑌾𑌟𑍍𑌸𑍂𑌨𑍁𑌰𑍍𑌮𑌹𑍇𑌶𑌾𑌹𑍍𑌵𑌯𑍋  
𑌵𑌿𑌦𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌤𑍀𑌰𑍍𑌥𑌪𑌦𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌨𑌿𑌯𑌮𑍍𑌯 𑌸𑌮𑌯𑍇𑌷𑍍𑌵𑌦𑍍𑌵𑍈𑌤𑌮𑍁𑌦𑍍𑌦𑍍𑌯𑍋𑌤𑌯𑌨𑍍।  
𑌅𑌧𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌸𑍍𑌤 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌤𑌿𑌕𑌾𑌮𑌕𑍋𑌟𑌿 𑌶𑌰𑌦𑍋 𑌦𑍍𑌵𑌾𑌤𑍍𑌰𑌿𑌂𑌶𑌤𑌂 𑌦𑍇𑌹𑌿𑌨𑌾𑌂  
𑌦𑍍𑌵𑍈𑌤𑌧𑍍𑌵𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌨𑌿𑌵𑌾𑌰𑌣𑍋 𑌨𑌵𑌮𑌠𑍀𑌨𑌾𑌥𑍋 𑌨𑌵𑌃 𑌶𑌙𑍍𑌕𑌰𑌃॥௧௦௩॥  
𑌸 𑌦𑍁𑌰𑍍𑌮𑍁𑌖𑌿𑌨𑌿 𑌸𑌨𑍍𑌮𑍁𑌖𑍋 𑌮𑌧𑍁𑌰𑌵𑌾𑌙𑍍𑌮𑌧𑍌 𑌮𑍌𑌨𑌿𑌰𑌾𑌟𑍍  
𑌪𑌦𑍀 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌤𑌿𑌪𑌦𑌿 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌗𑍇 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌸𑌿𑌤𑌧𑍀𑌃 𑌸𑌿𑌤𑍇 𑌪𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌕𑍇।  
𑌸𑌮𑌸𑍍𑌤𑌭𑍁𑌵𑌨𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌚𑌿𑌤𑌃 𑌸𑌕𑍃𑌦𑍍 𑌉𑌮𑍇𑌶𑌯𑌨𑍍 𑌅𑌚𑍍𑌯𑍁𑌤𑌂  
𑌜𑌹𑍌 𑌤𑌨𑍁𑌮𑌨𑍁𑌤𑍍𑌤𑌮𑌾𑌮𑍍 𑌅𑌵𑌿𑌶𑌦𑍍 𑌆𑌶𑍁 𑌨𑍈𑌜𑌂 𑌮𑌹𑌃॥௧௦௪॥  
—𑌪𑍁𑌣𑍍𑌯𑌶𑍍𑌲𑍋𑌕𑌮𑌞𑍍𑌜𑌰𑍀

4be334816e.d:
On this day, remnants of LTTE territory were overrun by Lankan Sinhala military, culminating the months long massive massacre of Tamil Hindu civilians lured into "safe no-fire zones" and shelled / bombed. Remnants were raped, murdered and filmed by Lankan soldiers. The LTTE had used a fraction of these civilians as human shields, forced labor and child soldiers.

In preperation for the slaughter, in Sep 2008, Lankans had ordered all international (including UN) observers out. They then made false promises of safe zones and not using heavy weapons. Then they closed in and slaughtered. 

The SLA assault employed aerial bombardment, long-range artillery, howitzers and MBRLs as well as small mortars, RPGs and small arms fire, some of it fired from a close range. 

Soldiers claimed that they had been ordered to kill all tamils, including civilians. Lankan Defence Secretary Gotabhaya Rajapaksa, President Rajapaksa's brother, was said to have given direct orders to army commanders at the battle front (Gen. Sarath Fonseka claimed it as well). He'd even foiled the leaders' surrender attempts.

Aftermath
An internal UN report in 2012 revised that estimate to at least 70,000 civilians. Population data from the World Bank indicates that over 100,000 Tamils remain unaccounted for from the final months of the war.

Survivors were forced into camps, many more died and were raped/ tortured.

Some documentaries were made (eg. "No Fire Zone"), reports published. Lankan Tamils and diaspora commemorate the Mullivaikkal Remembrance Day. Perpetrators were not punished.

Buddhist sinhalese harrassment of hindu tamils continued unabated over the next decades.


**Context**  
Sinhalese were jealous of colonial era Tamil success and dominance. So, they brought in the Sinhala Only Act 1956. By 1972, with the "policy of standardization", they restricted tamil entry to universities and jobs. There were Sinhala riots; leading to tamil rebel groups. Added to this was old religious hatred towards Hindus.

4beb4fe26d.d:
On this night, Muslim Kashmiri soldiers led by Major Nasarullah Khan brutally massaccred their Hindu fellows (some in their sleep) and joined Pakistani Islamist invaders.

Killing 
On the night of 15/16 October 1947, a large party of raiders laid siege to Tharochi Fort where two companies of 2 J&K Battalion, one Gorkha and one Muslim had taken refuge. Brigadier Chhattar Singh in command of the Mirpur Brigade ordered his Brigade Major (BM), Major Nasarullah Khan to take two platoons of 3 JAK Battalion to deliver supplies and ammunition to the garrison in the Fort. 

#The garrison
On the way, he also assumed command of two companies sent earlier to relieve the besieged garrison. He deployed the Muslim Company on perimeter defense duty outside the Fort and told the Gorkhas to rest. Nasarullah Khan then called a meeting of all Muslim officers and JCOs and hatched a plan to eliminate the non-Muslim elements. During the night, the Muslim Company mercilessly butchered the sleeping Gorkhas! The Gorkha Commander, Captain Prem Singh was strangled to death by Muslim brother officers of his own battalion. Two Gorkha JCOs and 30 Other Ranks (OR) managed to escape the massacre.

#The fort
Major Nasarullah Khan then led the Muslim troops inside the Tharochhi Fort where the garrison, was unaware of the developments of the night before and received the relieving column with joy. And at night, the unsuspecting Gorkhas were all murdered in a repeat performance. Their commander, Captain Raghubir Singh Thapa was tortured to death!

Context
Such betrayal by almost all the Muslim soldiers in the Maharaja’s army led to the crisis which followed.

4c4117042b.b: Observed on Puṣyaḥ nakshatra of Vr̥ṣabhaḥ (sidereal solar) month (Prātaḥ/paraviddha).
4c4117042b.d:
Between the 6th and 9th centuries, in South India, there existed 63 ardent devotees of Bhagavan Shiva, collectively known as the Nayanmars. These devout individuals, hailing from various walks of life including potters, fishermen, farmers, merchants, priests, hunters, and washermen, created devotional songs still sung by followers around the globe. Among these Nayanmars, Appar, Sambandar, and Sundarar, known for their Thevaram hymns, along with Manikkavasagar, are distinguished as the Samayacharyas or the ‘The Four’ (nālvar) revered teachers of the faith. They were instrumental in promoting the Shaiva Siddhanta philosophy and culture, effectively challenging the spread of Jainism and Buddhism. Their teachings centered around the concept that Shiva embodies love, and that embracing love for all beings and existence is essential in connecting with Shiva, the Supreme Being.

Nami Nandi Adigal, a devout Brahmana from Emaperur in the Chola kingdom, dedicated his life to worshipping Bhagavan Shiva in Tiruvarur. One day, driven by a desire to light numerous lamps in the temple as extolled in the Shiva Agamas, he sought ghee from a nearby house. However, the Jaina inhabitant mockingly suggested using water instead. Distressed, Nandi Adigal prayed to Bhagavan Shiva and was divinely instructed to use water from a nearby tank for lighting the lamps. Miraculously, the lamps burned brightly with water, astonishing the Jainas and leading to a decline in Jainism as people turned to Shaivism.

Recognising his devotion, the Chola king appointed Nandi Adigal as the head of the temple. He zealously conducted the Panguni Uttaram festival at Tirumanali, drawing worshippers of all varṇas. One night, feeling unpurified by the contact with people of various varṇas, he hesitated to enter his home. As he waited for his wife to bring him water to bathe, he fell asleep and dreamt of Bhagavan Shiva, who revealed that all born in Tiruvarur were His ganas! Awakening, Nandi Adigal narrated this story to his wife, and performed his worship. In the morning, he went back to Tiruvarur and saw that the people of Tiruvarur bore the form of Bhagavan Shiva! As he prostrated to them, they all resumed their original forms --- thus a divine Lila being enacted by Bhagavan.

Settling in Tiruvarur, Nandi Adigal devoted himself to serving Bhagavan and His devotees, earning praise as 'Anipon' (pure gold) from the Nayanmar Appar. He ultimately attained the sublime abode of Bhagavan Shiva, exemplifying pure devotion and service.

4c5b681762.b: Graha-yuddha (amshu-vimarda) between guruḥ and budhaḥ in puṣyaḥ karkaṭaḥ, center-to-center separation 0°33′09.53″.
4c5b681762.d:
This is an amshu-vimarda (a collision of rays -- the discs themselves do not touch): center-to-center separation 0°33′09.53″, 0°32′51.38″ apart, disc-to-disc. guruḥ at puṣyaḥ-4 karkaṭaḥ (latitude 0°29′56.67″ N, Rju (direct), magnitude -1.79, elongation 12°31′25.23″ W). budhaḥ at puṣyaḥ-4 karkaṭaḥ (latitude 1°03′06.20″ N, Rju (direct), magnitude -1.26, elongation 12°33′26.54″ W). Classical texts weigh both the northern position and the greater apparent brightness/nearness in deciding the victor (jayI) of a yuddha; here budhaḥ is towards the north (traditionally said to prevail), while by brightness/nearness (the larger apparent diameter) guruḥ is taken as jayI over budhaḥ. A graha-yuddha (also called amshu-vimarda, "collision of rays") occurs when two of the five tArA grahas -- budha, śukra, aṅgāraka, br̥haspati, śanaiśchara -- come within 1 aMsha (60 kalA) of each other in longitude, close enough that they may be difficult to tell apart in the sky. It is called yuddha proper only when their discs actually touch/overlap; otherwise, amshu-vimarda.

The Surya Siddhanta itself cautions that this matter is described only to indicate the auspicious/inauspicious effects for people -- in reality the grahas remain far apart from one another and continue along their own paths. This is not to be received with fear, but as an advance, compassionate intimation from those who calculated these movements accurately, meant to help people take protective measures in time.

Classical texts (e.g. Brihat Samhita ch. 17) weigh both which graha is to the north and which is more prominent (nearer/brighter, of larger apparent diameter) in declaring a victor (jayī) of the yuddha; the defeated (jita) graha's significations are said to suffer for a particular section of society -- this is never a universal ill effect. The traditional response is to increase one's spiritual efforts: japa, homa, dAna and parAyaNa (especially of the Navagraha stotra), with higher AvRtti for the two grahas actually involved, particularly if the day also coincides with some other puNya kAla (e.g. a sAyana saGkramaNa).

Per the Narada Samhita (as cited in Muhurta Chintamani), the nakshatra in which a graha-yuddha occurs should be avoided for auspicious functions (vivAha, upanayana etc.) for six months following the event. If this cannot be avoided, perform parihAra for candra-bala.

4cc5ee5b45.d: He, Soma, initiated with the title Bodhendra by the preceptor Paraśivendra adorned the Pīṭha and visiting countries in the palanquin exquisitely decked with gems offered by Bhoja, the king of Dhārā, inculcating faith in the principles of Advaita in the minds of those who venerated him on the path safeguarded the Maṭha from the invaders (mlechas) with the help of the minister of the Kashmiri King Kalaśa.  Having stayed in the Pīṭha for thirty-seven years, He reached the Supreme Abode at Aruṇācala on the New moon day of the month Āṣāḍha in the year Īśvara. This preceptor Bodhendra, also known as Sānandrānanda, was honoured for poetical excellence by Kings—Bhoja, Kalaśeśvara and others and was intent on travelling through the earth.

4cd2f38c95.b: Graha-yuddha (amshu-vimarda) between aṅgārakaḥ and budhaḥ in uttarāṣāḍhā makaraḥ, center-to-center separation 0°41′01.91″.
4cd2f38c95.d:
This is an amshu-vimarda (a collision of rays -- the discs themselves do not touch): center-to-center separation 0°41′01.91″, 0°40′57.05″ apart, disc-to-disc. aṅgārakaḥ at uttarāṣāḍhā-4 makaraḥ (latitude 1°06′36.60″ S, Rju (direct), magnitude +1.17, elongation 16°01′11.62″ E). budhaḥ at uttarāṣāḍhā-4 makaraḥ (latitude 1°47′38.51″ S, Rju (direct), magnitude -0.85, elongation 16°04′48.50″ E). Classical texts weigh both the northern position and the greater apparent brightness/nearness in deciding the victor (jayI) of a yuddha; here budhaḥ is towards the north (traditionally said to prevail), while by brightness/nearness (the larger apparent diameter) budhaḥ is taken as jayI over aṅgārakaḥ. A graha-yuddha (also called amshu-vimarda, "collision of rays") occurs when two of the five tArA grahas -- budha, śukra, aṅgāraka, br̥haspati, śanaiśchara -- come within 1 aMsha (60 kalA) of each other in longitude, close enough that they may be difficult to tell apart in the sky. It is called yuddha proper only when their discs actually touch/overlap; otherwise, amshu-vimarda.

The Surya Siddhanta itself cautions that this matter is described only to indicate the auspicious/inauspicious effects for people -- in reality the grahas remain far apart from one another and continue along their own paths. This is not to be received with fear, but as an advance, compassionate intimation from those who calculated these movements accurately, meant to help people take protective measures in time.

Classical texts (e.g. Brihat Samhita ch. 17) weigh both which graha is to the north and which is more prominent (nearer/brighter, of larger apparent diameter) in declaring a victor (jayī) of the yuddha; the defeated (jita) graha's significations are said to suffer for a particular section of society -- this is never a universal ill effect. The traditional response is to increase one's spiritual efforts: japa, homa, dAna and parAyaNa (especially of the Navagraha stotra), with higher AvRtti for the two grahas actually involved, particularly if the day also coincides with some other puNya kAla (e.g. a sAyana saGkramaNa).

Per the Narada Samhita (as cited in Muhurta Chintamani), the nakshatra in which a graha-yuddha occurs should be avoided for auspicious functions (vivAha, upanayana etc.) for six months following the event. If this cannot be avoided, perform parihAra for candra-bala.

4d2199e65e.b: Graha-yuddha (amshu-vimarda) between guruḥ and śukraḥ in ārdrā mithunam, center-to-center separation 0°51′45.60″.
4d2199e65e.d:
This is an amshu-vimarda (a collision of rays -- the discs themselves do not touch): center-to-center separation 0°51′45.60″, 0°51′22.65″ apart, disc-to-disc. guruḥ at ārdrā-4 mithunam (latitude 0°03′51.48″ S, Rju (direct), magnitude -1.94, elongation 35°43′03.64″ W). śukraḥ at ārdrā-4 mithunam (latitude 0°55′37.08″ S, Rju (direct), magnitude -3.96, elongation 35°43′40.87″ W). Classical texts weigh both the northern position and the greater apparent brightness/nearness in deciding the victor (jayI) of a yuddha; here śukraḥ is towards the north (traditionally said to prevail), while by brightness/nearness (the larger apparent diameter) guruḥ is taken as jayI over śukraḥ. A graha-yuddha (also called amshu-vimarda, "collision of rays") occurs when two of the five tArA grahas -- budha, śukra, aṅgāraka, br̥haspati, śanaiśchara -- come within 1 aMsha (60 kalA) of each other in longitude, close enough that they may be difficult to tell apart in the sky. It is called yuddha proper only when their discs actually touch/overlap; otherwise, amshu-vimarda.

The Surya Siddhanta itself cautions that this matter is described only to indicate the auspicious/inauspicious effects for people -- in reality the grahas remain far apart from one another and continue along their own paths. This is not to be received with fear, but as an advance, compassionate intimation from those who calculated these movements accurately, meant to help people take protective measures in time.

Classical texts (e.g. Brihat Samhita ch. 17) weigh both which graha is to the north and which is more prominent (nearer/brighter, of larger apparent diameter) in declaring a victor (jayī) of the yuddha; the defeated (jita) graha's significations are said to suffer for a particular section of society -- this is never a universal ill effect. The traditional response is to increase one's spiritual efforts: japa, homa, dAna and parAyaNa (especially of the Navagraha stotra), with higher AvRtti for the two grahas actually involved, particularly if the day also coincides with some other puNya kAla (e.g. a sAyana saGkramaNa).

Per the Narada Samhita (as cited in Muhurta Chintamani), the nakshatra in which a graha-yuddha occurs should be avoided for auspicious functions (vivAha, upanayana etc.) for six months following the event. If this cannot be avoided, perform parihAra for candra-bala.

4d3dd8f4ef.d:
In an event that shook the marATha empire, the peshva nArayaNa rAv, brother of the great mAdhavarAv and vishvAs-rAv, was killed on the last day of gaNapati festival (Ananta Chaturdashi) in puNe.

Context
raghunAth rAv, though having military talent, was a power-hungry unscrupulous person with traitorous tendencies. He had earlier tried to usurp the throne from mAdhav rAv, only to be outmaneouvered and subdued with great difficulty by that noble peshva. With his death, raghoba was back at his old game.

Events
According to popular legend, Raghunathrao had sent a message to Sumer Singh Gardi to fetch Narayanrao using the Marathi word dharaa (धरा) or 'hold' (actual phrase in Marathi - " नारायणरावांना धरा"/"Narayanrao-ana dhara"). This message was intercepted by his wife Anandibai who changed a single letter to make it read as maaraa (मारा) or 'kill' . The miscommunication led the Gardis to chase Narayanrao, who, upon hearing them coming, started running towards his uncles' residence screaming, "Kaka! Mala Vachva!!" ("Uncle! Save me!"). The Gardis followed Narayanrao to his uncle's chamber and the menial Tulaji Pawar pulled him while Sumer Singh Gardi cut him down. At the scene, a total of 11 persons were killed. Historian Sardesai writes that these 11 victims included seven brahmins (including Narayanrao), two Maratha servants and two maids.

Aftermath
The Chief Justice, Ram Shastri Prabhune was asked to conduct an investigation into the incident, and Raghunathrao, Anandibai and Sumer Singh Gardi were all prosecuted in absentia. Although Raghunathrao was acquitted, Anandibai was declared an offender and Sumer Singh Gardi the culprit. Sumer Singh Gardi died mysteriously in Patna, Bihar in 1775, and Anandibai performed Hindu rituals to absolve her sins. Kharag Singh and Tulaji Pawar were handed over by Hyder Ali back to the government and they were tortured to death.

As the result of the murder, senior ministers and generals of the Maratha confederacy formed a regency council, known as the "Baarbhai Council", to conduct of the affairs of the state in the name of his soon to be born son, mAdhavarAv 2.

--𑌸𑍂𑌰𑍍𑌯𑌸𑌿𑌦𑍍𑌧𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌤𑍇

4e24eeb0cf.b: Observed on Śukla-Tr̥tīyā tithi of Caitraḥ (lunar) month (Madhyāhnaḥ/puurvaviddha).

4e26c2d1e5.d:
On this day, shabarImala temple was found desecrated. Police report (by DIG KK Menon) suspected Christians.

First noticed by a priest on June 14, 1950, the arson was reported to police two days later by the commissioner and the president of Travancore Devaswom Board. The temple was last closed on May 20. The priest, his subordinates and some worshippers had left the place, with nobody staying back. When Kollam district superintendent of police visited the place, he had noticed that, “The idol was found broken; the head, left hand palm and fingers separated. There were cut marks on the face of the idol as well as on the forehead.” The enquiry had found out that the fire was not an accident. There were 15 cut marks of violence on the door leading to the sreekovil (sanctum sanctorum), indicating forcible entry, the report said. Police had found traces of brass on the sharp edge of an axe found from the spot. Theft attempt was ruled out as silver, gold and utensils were not taken away.

Aftermath: The temple was rebuilt, the stone idol replaced with a metal one.

𑌕𑍁𑌶𑍋𑌤𑍍𑌪𑌾𑌟𑌨𑌮𑌨𑍍𑌤𑍍𑌰𑌸𑍍𑌤𑍁---

𑌅𑌥 𑌕𑍁𑌶𑍋𑌤𑍍𑌪𑌾𑌟𑌨𑍇𑌽𑌨𑍍𑌯𑌸𑍍𑌮𑍃𑌤𑌿𑌲𑌿𑌖𑌿𑌤𑌮𑌨𑍍𑌤𑍍𑌰𑌃---  
𑍐 𑌵𑌿𑌰𑌞𑍍𑌚𑌿𑌨𑌾 𑌸𑌹𑍋𑌤𑍍𑌪𑌨𑍍𑌨 𑌪𑌰𑌮𑍇𑌷𑍍𑌠𑌿𑌨𑌿𑌸𑌰𑍍𑌗𑌜।

4e6ba2860f.b: Event occured on 1520-05-29 (gregorian). Julian date was converted to Gregorian in this reckoning.
4e6ba2860f.d:
Krishnadeva Raya of Vijayanagar routed the Bijapur army of Ismail Adil Shah which had come to save Raichur fort (beseiged since around March) and captured it.

Ismail hoped that his artillery would decimate Vijayanagara attackers - but Krishnadevaraya only sent a division under kumAra vijaya for a vigorous attack. As the bijApur vanguard retreated, the artillery opened fire forcing kumAra vijaya's forces to retreat - pursued by bijApur forces. At that time, the rAya joined with the rest of his army crushing the pursuers. bijApur army fled - many drowned in the kRShNA river at their rear. Salabat Khan tried to stop the rout, but his band of 500 portuguese mercenaries were eliminated and Salabat captured as they almost reached the rAya's guard. Adil Shah, who did not fight at all, ran away on an elephant with 500 horse. Horse trader Christovao de Figueiredo then offered services of his band of 20 - they picked off fort defenders (including the governor) using their arquebusses. After that the fort was captured.  

Context:  Vijayanagara had captured rAyachUru earlier in 1510, but they'd lost it in 1516 while busy fighting gajapati-s. Krishnadevaraya, aged 35, sent Seyed Maraikar, a Muslim in his service, to Goa with 40k gold coins to buy horses. Maraikar betrayed Krishnadevaraya's cause and went to Ismail Adil Shah with the money and offered his services. Krishnadevaraya made a demand that Maraikar be returned along with the money. Ismail refused and instead helped him escape to Goa. During the period of peace Krishnadevaraya made extensive preparations for a grand attack on Raichur Doab. After the court decided that Raichur should be attacked, the king invited all commanders (Nayakas) in his service to take part in the battle.

Aftermath: Nizam Shah, Qutb Shah, Barid Shah and Imad Shah wrote to the rAya asking him to return rAyachUru or that they would combine against him. The rAya replied that they should not trouble themselves - he would visit them. Ismail dallied until the rAya marched on to bijApur itself (1523). Sadly, just 7 years later, aged 45, kRShNadevarAya died even as he planned to capture beLgaum.

4e78a4ac01.b: Event occured on 0485-04-18 (gregorian). Julian date was converted to Gregorian in this reckoning.
4e78a4ac01.d:
The yavana polytheist sage died in Athens on this date in 485 CE. Proclus died aged 73, and was buried near Mount Lycabettus in a tomb. It is reported that he was writing 700 lines each day.

He had a great devotion to the goddess Athena, who he believed guided him at key moments in his life. Marinus reports that when Christians removed the statue of the goddess from the Parthenon, a beautiful woman appeared to Proclus in a dream and announced that the "Athenian Lady" wished to stay at his home.

4e794466de.s:
𑌅𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌯𑍍𑌯𑌤𑍃𑌤𑍀𑌯𑌾 𑌵𑍈𑌶𑌾𑌖𑌶𑍁𑌕𑍍𑌲𑌤𑍃𑌤𑍀𑌯𑌾𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌨𑌿𑌰𑍍𑌣𑌯𑌾𑌮𑍃𑌤𑍇 𑌭𑌵𑌿𑌷𑍍𑌯𑍇 𑌵𑌿𑌷𑍍𑌣𑍁𑌪𑍂𑌜𑍋𑌕𑍍𑌤𑌾---  
𑌵𑍈𑌶𑌾𑌖𑌸𑍍𑌯 𑌤𑍃𑌤𑍀𑌯𑌾𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌶𑍍𑌰𑍀𑌸𑌮𑍇𑌤𑌂 𑌜𑌗𑌦𑍍𑌗𑍁𑌰𑍁𑌮𑍍।  
𑌨𑌾𑌰𑌾𑌯𑌣𑌂 𑌪𑍂𑌜𑌯𑍇𑌤 𑌪𑍁𑌷𑍍𑌪𑌧𑍂𑌪𑌵𑌿𑌲𑍇𑌪𑌨𑍈𑌃।  
𑌤𑌤𑍍𑌰𑍈𑌵 𑌵𑌿𑌶𑍇𑌷𑌃---  
𑌵𑍈𑌶𑌾𑌖𑍇 𑌶𑍁𑌕𑍍𑌲𑌪𑌕𑍍𑌷𑍇 𑌚 𑌤𑍃𑌤𑍀𑌯𑌾𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌤𑌥𑍈𑌵 𑌚।  
𑌗𑌙𑍍𑌗𑌾𑌤𑍋𑌯𑍈𑌰𑍍𑌨𑌰𑌃 𑌸𑍍𑌨𑌾𑌤𑍍𑌵𑌾 𑌮𑍁𑌚𑍍𑌯𑌤𑍇 𑌸𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌕𑌿𑌲𑍍𑌬𑌿𑌷𑍈𑌃।  
𑌤𑌸𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌕𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌯𑍋 𑌯𑌵𑍈𑌰𑍍𑌹𑍋𑌮𑍋 𑌯𑌵𑍈𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌿𑌷𑍍𑌣𑍁𑌂 𑌸𑌮𑌰𑍍𑌚𑌯𑍇𑌤𑍍।  
𑌯𑌵𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌦𑌦𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌦𑍍 𑌦𑍍𑌵𑌿𑌜𑌾𑌤𑌿𑌭𑍍𑌯𑌃 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌯𑌤𑌃 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌶𑌯𑌦𑍍𑌯𑌵𑌾𑌨𑍍।  
𑌤𑌥𑌾 𑌮𑌦𑌨𑌰𑌤𑍍𑌨𑍇 𑌭𑌵𑌿𑌷𑍍𑌯𑍇---  
𑌕𑍃𑌷𑍍𑌣 𑌉𑌵𑌾𑌚  
𑌬𑌹𑍁𑌨𑌾𑌽𑌤𑍍𑌰 𑌕𑌿𑌮𑍁𑌕𑍍𑌤𑍇𑌨 𑌕𑌿𑌂 𑌬𑌹𑍍𑌵𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌰𑌮𑌾𑌲𑌯𑌾।  
𑌵𑍈𑌶𑌾𑌖𑌸𑍍𑌯 𑌸𑌿𑌤𑌾𑌮𑍇𑌕𑌾𑌂 𑌤𑍃𑌤𑍀𑌯𑌾𑌮𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌶𑍃𑌣𑍁॥௧॥  
𑌯𑌸𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌸𑍍𑌨𑌾𑌨𑌂 𑌜𑌪𑍋 𑌹𑍋𑌮𑌃 𑌸𑍍𑌵𑌾𑌧𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌯𑌃 𑌪𑌿𑌤𑍃𑌤𑌰𑍍𑌪𑌣𑌮𑍍।  
𑌦𑌾𑌨𑌂 𑌚 𑌕𑍍𑌰𑌿𑌯𑌤𑍇 𑌕𑌿𑌞𑍍𑌚𑌿𑌤𑍍 𑌤𑌤𑍍𑌸𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌂 𑌸𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌦𑌿𑌹𑌾𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌯𑌮𑍍॥௨॥  
𑌆𑌦𑌿𑌃 𑌕𑍃𑌤𑌯𑍁𑌗𑌸𑍍𑌯𑍇𑌯𑌂 𑌯𑍁𑌗𑌾𑌦𑌿𑌸𑍍𑌤𑍇𑌨 𑌕𑌥𑍍𑌯𑌤𑍇।  
𑌸𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌪𑌾𑌪𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌶𑌮𑌨𑍀 𑌸𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌸𑍌𑌖𑍍𑌯𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌦𑌾𑌯𑌿𑌨𑍀॥௩॥  
𑌪𑍁𑌰𑌾 𑌮𑌹𑍋𑌦𑌯𑍇 𑌪𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌥 𑌵𑌣𑌿𑌗𑌾𑌸𑍀𑌤𑍍𑌸 𑌨𑌿𑌰𑍍𑌧𑌨𑌃।  
𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌿𑌯𑌂𑌵𑌦𑌃 𑌸𑌤𑍍𑌯𑌵𑍃𑌤𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌰𑍍𑌦𑍇𑌵𑌬𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌹𑍍𑌮𑌣𑌪𑍂𑌜𑌕𑌃॥௪॥  
𑌪𑍁𑌣𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌖𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌨𑍈𑌕𑌚𑌿𑌤𑍍𑌤𑍋𑌽𑌭𑍂𑌤𑍍𑌕𑍁𑌟𑍁𑌮𑍍𑌬𑌵𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌕𑍁𑌲𑍋𑌽𑌪𑌿 𑌸𑌨𑍍।  
𑌤𑍇𑌨 𑌶𑍍𑌰𑍁𑌤𑌾 𑌵𑌾𑌚𑍍𑌯𑌮𑌾𑌨𑌾 𑌤𑍃𑌤𑍀𑌯𑌾 𑌰𑍋𑌹𑌿𑌣𑍀𑌯𑍁𑌤𑌾॥௫॥  
𑌯𑌦𑌾 𑌸𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌦𑍍 𑌬𑍁𑌧𑌸𑌂𑌯𑍁𑌕𑍍𑌤𑌾 𑌤𑌦𑌾 𑌸𑌾 𑌸𑍁𑌮𑌹𑌾𑌫𑌲𑌾।  
𑌤𑌸𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌯𑌦𑍍𑌦𑍀𑌯𑌤𑍇 𑌕𑌿𑌞𑍍𑌚𑌿𑌦𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌯𑌂 𑌸𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌤𑍍𑌤𑌦𑍇𑌵 𑌹𑌿॥௬॥  
𑌇𑌤𑌿 𑌶𑍍𑌰𑍁𑌤𑍍𑌵𑌾 𑌸 𑌗𑌙𑍍𑌗𑌾𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌸𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌰𑍍𑌪𑍍𑌯 𑌪𑌿𑌤𑍃𑌦𑍇𑌵𑌤𑌾𑌃।  
𑌗𑍃𑌹𑌮𑌾𑌗𑌤𑍍𑌯 𑌕𑌰𑌕𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌸𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌨𑌾𑌨𑍁𑌦𑌕𑌸𑌂𑌯𑍁𑌤𑌾𑌨𑍍॥௭॥  
𑌅𑌨𑍍𑌨𑌪𑍂𑌰𑍍𑌣𑌾𑌨𑍍 𑌬𑍃𑌹𑌤𑍍𑌕𑍁𑌮𑍍𑌭𑌾𑌞𑍍𑌜𑌲𑍇𑌨 𑌵𑌿𑌮𑌲𑍇𑌨 𑌚।  
𑌯𑌵𑌗𑍋𑌧𑍂𑌮𑌚𑌣𑌕𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌸𑌕𑍍𑌤𑍂𑌨𑍍𑌦𑌧𑍍𑌯𑍋𑌦𑌨𑌂 𑌤𑌥𑌾॥௮॥  
𑌇𑌕𑍍𑌷𑍁𑌕𑍍𑌷𑍀𑌰𑌵𑌿𑌕𑌾𑌰𑌾𑌂𑌶𑍍𑌚 𑌸𑌹𑌿𑌰𑌣𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌂𑌶𑍍𑌚 𑌶𑌕𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌤𑌃।  
𑌶𑍁𑌚𑌿𑌃 𑌶𑍁𑌦𑍍𑌧𑍇𑌨 𑌮𑌨𑌸𑌾 𑌬𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌹𑍍𑌮𑌣𑍇𑌭𑍍𑌯𑍋 𑌦𑌦𑍌 𑌵𑌣𑌿𑌕𑍍॥௯॥  
𑌭𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌯𑌯𑌾 𑌵𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌯𑌮𑌾𑌣𑍋𑌽𑌪𑌿 𑌕𑍁𑌟𑍁𑌮𑍍𑌬𑌾𑌸𑌕𑍍𑌤𑌚𑌿𑌤𑍍𑌤𑌯𑌾।  
𑌤𑌾𑌵𑌤𑍍𑌤𑌸𑍍𑌥𑍌 𑌸𑍍𑌥𑌿𑌰𑍇 𑌸𑌤𑍍𑌤𑍍𑌵𑍇 𑌮𑌤𑍍𑌵𑌾 𑌸𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌂 𑌵𑌿𑌨𑌶𑍍𑌵𑌰𑌮𑍍॥௧௦॥  
𑌧𑌰𑍍𑌮𑌾𑌸𑌕𑍍𑌤𑌮𑌤𑌿𑌃 𑌪𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌥𑍇 𑌕𑌾𑌲𑍇𑌨 𑌬𑌹𑍁𑌨𑌾 𑌤𑌤𑌃।  
𑌜𑌗𑌾𑌮 𑌪𑌞𑍍𑌚𑌤𑍍𑌵𑌮𑌸𑍌 𑌵𑌾𑌸𑍁𑌦𑍇𑌵𑌮𑌨𑍁𑌸𑍍𑌮𑌰𑌨𑍍॥௧௧॥  
𑌤𑌤𑌃 𑌸 𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌤𑍍𑌰𑌿𑌯𑍋 𑌜𑌾𑌤𑌃 𑌕𑍁𑌶𑌾𑌵𑌤𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌯𑍁𑌧𑌿𑌷𑍍𑌠𑌿𑌰।  
𑌬𑌭𑍂𑌵 𑌚𑌾𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌯𑌾 𑌤𑌸𑍍𑌯 𑌸𑌮𑍃𑌦𑍍𑌧𑌿𑌰𑍍𑌧𑌰𑍍𑌮𑌸𑌂𑌯𑍁𑌤𑌾॥௧௨॥  
𑌇𑌯𑌾𑌜 𑌸 𑌮𑌹𑌾𑌯𑌜𑍍𑌞𑍈𑌃 𑌸𑌮𑌾𑌪𑍍𑌤𑌵𑌰𑌦𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌿𑌣𑍈𑌃।  
𑌸 𑌦𑌦𑍌 𑌗𑍋𑌹𑌿𑌰𑌣𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌦𑌿 𑌦𑌾𑌨𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌯𑌨𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌯𑌹𑌰𑍍𑌨𑌿𑌶𑌮𑍍॥௧௩॥  
𑌬𑍁𑌭𑍁𑌜𑍇 𑌕𑌾𑌮𑌤𑍋 𑌭𑍋𑌗𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌦𑍀𑌨𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌧𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌪𑍂𑌰𑌯𑌦𑍍𑌧𑌨𑍈𑌃।  
𑌤𑌥𑌾𑌽𑌪𑍍𑌯𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌯𑌮𑍇𑌵𑌾𑌸𑍍𑌯 𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌯𑌂 𑌯𑌾𑌤𑌿 𑌨 𑌤𑌦𑍍𑌧𑌨𑌮𑍍॥௧௪॥  
𑌶𑍍𑌰𑌦𑍍𑌧𑌾𑌪𑍂𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌂 𑌤𑍃𑌤𑍀𑌯𑌾𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌦𑌤𑍍𑌤𑌂 𑌚 𑌵𑌿𑌭𑌵𑌂 𑌵𑌿𑌨𑌾।  
𑌇𑌤𑍍𑌯𑍇𑌤𑌤𑍍𑌤𑍇 𑌸𑌮𑌾𑌖𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌤𑌂 𑌶𑍍𑌰𑍂𑌯𑌤𑌾𑌮𑌤𑍍𑌰 𑌯𑍋 𑌵𑌿𑌧𑌿𑌃॥௧௫॥  
𑌤𑍃𑌤𑍀𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌚 𑌸𑌮𑌾𑌸𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌯 𑌸𑍍𑌨𑌾𑌤𑍍𑌵𑌾 𑌸𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌰𑍍𑌪𑍍𑌯 𑌦𑍇𑌵𑌤𑌾𑌃।  
𑌏𑌕𑌭𑌕𑍍𑌤𑌂 𑌤𑌦𑌾 𑌕𑍁𑌰𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌵𑌾𑌸𑍁𑌦𑍇𑌵𑌂 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌪𑍂𑌜𑌯𑍇𑌤𑍍॥௧௬॥   
𑌉𑌦𑌕𑍁𑌮𑍍𑌭𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌸𑌕𑌰𑌕𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌸𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌨𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌸𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌰𑌸𑍈𑌃 𑌸𑌹।  
𑌗𑍍𑌰𑍈𑌷𑍍𑌮𑌿𑌕𑌂 𑌸𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌮𑍇𑌵𑌾𑌤𑍍𑌰 𑌸𑌸𑍍𑌯𑌂 𑌦𑌾𑌨𑍇 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌶𑌸𑍍𑌯𑌤𑍇॥௧௭॥   
𑌛𑌤𑍍𑌰𑍋𑌪𑌾𑌨𑌤𑍍𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌦𑌾𑌨𑌂 𑌚 𑌗𑍋𑌭𑍂𑌕𑌾𑌶𑍍𑌵𑌨𑌵𑌾𑌸𑌸𑌾𑌮𑍍।  
𑌯𑌦𑍍𑌯𑌦𑌿𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌤𑌮𑌂 𑌚𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌯𑌤𑍍𑌤𑌦𑍍𑌦𑍇𑌯𑌮𑌵𑌿𑌶𑌙𑍍𑌕𑌯𑌾॥௧௮॥   
𑌏𑌤𑌤𑍍𑌤𑍇 𑌸𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌮𑌾𑌖𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌤𑌂 𑌕𑌿𑌮𑌨𑍍𑌯𑌚𑍍𑌛𑍍𑌰𑍋𑌤𑍁𑌮𑌿𑌚𑍍𑌛𑌸𑌿।  
𑌅𑌨𑌾𑌖𑍍𑌯𑍇𑌯𑌂 𑌨 𑌮𑍇 𑌕𑌿𑌞𑍍𑌚𑌿𑌦𑌸𑍍𑌤𑌿 𑌸𑍍𑌵𑌸𑍍𑌤𑍍𑌯𑌸𑍍𑌤𑍁 𑌤𑍇𑌽𑌨𑌘॥௧௯॥   
𑌅𑌸𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌤𑌿𑌥𑍌 𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌯𑌮𑍁𑌪𑍈𑌤𑌿 𑌹𑍁𑌤𑌂 𑌨 𑌦𑌤𑍍𑌤𑌂  
𑌤𑍇𑌨𑌾𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌯𑍇𑌤𑌿 𑌕𑌥𑌿𑌤𑌾 𑌮𑍁𑌨𑌿𑌭𑌿𑌸𑍍𑌤𑍃𑌤𑍀𑌯𑌾।  
𑌉𑌦𑍍𑌦𑌿𑌶𑍍𑌯 𑌦𑍈𑌵𑌤𑌪𑌿𑌤𑍄𑌨𑍍𑌕𑍍𑌰𑌿𑌯𑌤𑍇 𑌮𑌨𑍁𑌷𑍍𑌯𑍈𑌸𑍍-  
𑌤𑌚𑍍𑌚𑌾𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌯𑌂 𑌭𑌵𑌤𑌿 𑌭𑌾𑌰𑌤 𑌸𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌮𑍇𑌵॥௨௦॥  
  
𑌕𑍃𑌤𑍍𑌯𑌸𑌾𑌰𑌸𑌮𑍁𑌚𑍍𑌚𑌯𑍇---  
𑌅𑌥 𑌅𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌯𑌤𑍃𑌤𑍀𑌯𑌾 । 𑌵𑍈𑌶𑌾𑌖𑌶𑍁𑌕𑍍𑌲𑌤𑍃𑌤𑍀𑌯𑌾 𑌅𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌯𑌤𑍃𑌤𑍀𑌯𑌾, 𑌸𑌾 𑌚𑌤𑍁𑌰𑍍𑌥𑍀𑌯𑍁𑌕𑍍𑌤𑌾  
𑌗𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌹𑍍𑌯𑌾, 𑌤𑌥𑌾𑌹𑌿 𑌪𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌧𑌰𑍀𑌯𑌤𑌿𑌥𑌿𑌚𑌨𑍍𑌦𑍍𑌰𑌿𑌕𑌾𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌗𑍋𑌭𑌿𑌲𑌃-  
𑌵𑍈𑌶𑌾𑌖𑌸𑍍𑌯 𑌤𑍃𑌤𑍀𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌤𑍁 𑌪𑍂𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌵𑌿𑌦𑍍𑌧𑌾𑌂 𑌕𑌰𑍋𑌤𑌿 𑌯𑌃।  
𑌹𑌵𑍍𑌯𑌂 𑌦𑍇𑌵𑌾 𑌨 𑌗𑍃𑌹𑍍𑌣𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌿 𑌕𑌵𑍍𑌯𑌶𑍍𑌚 𑌪𑌿𑌤𑌰𑌸𑍍𑌤𑌥𑌾।  
𑌬𑍍𑌰𑌹𑍍𑌮𑌵𑍈𑌵𑌰𑍍𑌤𑍇---  
𑌰𑌮𑍍𑌭𑌾𑌖𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌵𑌰𑍍𑌜𑌯𑌿𑌤𑍍𑌵𑌾 𑌤𑍁 𑌤𑍃𑌤𑍀𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌦𑍍𑌵𑌿𑌜𑌸𑌤𑍍𑌤𑌮।  
𑌅𑌨𑍍𑌯𑍇𑌷𑍁 𑌸𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌕𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌯𑍇𑌷𑍁 𑌗𑌣𑌯𑍁𑌕𑍍𑌤𑌾 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌶𑌸𑍍𑌯𑌤𑍇॥ 𑌇𑌤𑌿।  
𑌗𑌣𑌯𑍁𑌕𑍍𑌤𑌾 𑌚𑌤𑍁𑌰𑍍𑌥𑍀𑌯𑍁𑌕𑍍𑌤𑌾, 𑌚𑌤𑍁𑌰𑍍𑌥𑍀𑌯𑍁𑌤𑌾𑌯𑌾 𑌅𑌲𑌾𑌭𑍇 𑌤𑍁 𑌦𑍍𑌵𑌿𑌤𑍀𑌯𑌾𑌯𑍁𑌤𑌾𑌽𑌪𑌿 𑌗𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌹𑍍𑌯𑌾।  
𑌬𑍍𑌰𑌹𑍍𑌮𑌪𑍁𑌰𑌾𑌣𑍇---  
𑌤𑌸𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌕𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌯𑍋 𑌯𑌵𑍈𑌰𑍍𑌯𑌜𑍍𑌞𑍋 𑌯𑌵𑍈𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌿𑌷𑍍𑌣𑍁𑌂 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌪𑍂𑌜𑌯𑍇𑌤𑍍।  
𑌯𑌵𑌾𑌨𑍍 𑌦𑌦𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌦𑍍 𑌦𑍍𑌵𑌿𑌜𑌾𑌤𑌿𑌭𑍍𑌯𑌃 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌯𑌤𑌃 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌶𑌯𑍇𑌦𑍍 𑌯𑌵𑌾𑌨𑍍॥  
𑌪𑍂𑌜𑌾𑌦𑌿 𑌵𑌿𑌧𑌾𑌯𑌾𑌤𑌿𑌶𑌯𑌿𑌤𑌾𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌯-𑌯𑌵𑌦𑌾𑌨-𑌜𑌨𑍍𑌯-𑌫𑌲-𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌪𑍍𑌤𑌿-𑌕𑌾𑌮𑌨𑌯𑌾 𑌯𑌵𑌾𑌨𑍍 𑌦𑌦𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌤𑍍।  
𑌤𑌦𑍍 𑌵𑌾𑌕𑍍𑌯𑌮𑍇𑌤𑌤𑍍 𑌫𑌲𑌾𑌨𑍁𑌸𑌾𑌰𑍇𑌣𑍋𑌹𑌯𑌂 (𑌕𑌰𑌣𑍀𑌯𑌮𑍍)। 𑌦𑍍𑌰𑌵𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌰𑌦𑌾𑌨𑍇𑌽𑌪𑌿  
𑌅𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌯𑌫𑌲𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌪𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌕𑌾𑌮𑌨𑌯𑌾 𑌇𑌤𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌦𑌿𑌵𑌾𑌕𑍍𑌯𑌮𑍍। 𑌨𑌾𑌰𑌦𑍀𑌯𑍇---  
𑌵𑍈𑌶𑌾𑌖𑍇 𑌶𑍁𑌕𑍍𑌲𑌪𑌕𑍍𑌷𑍇 𑌤𑍁 𑌤𑍃𑌤𑍀𑌯𑌾𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌤𑌥𑍈𑌵 𑌚।  
𑌗𑌙𑍍𑌗𑌾𑌤𑍋𑌯𑍇 𑌨𑌰𑌃 𑌸𑍍𑌨𑌾𑌤𑍍𑌵𑌾 𑌮𑍁𑌚𑍍𑌯𑌤𑍇 𑌸𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌕𑌿𑌲𑍍𑌬𑌿𑌷𑍈𑌃॥  
𑍐 𑌅𑌦𑍍𑌯𑍇𑌤𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌦𑌿 𑌸𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌕𑌿𑌲𑍍𑌬𑌿𑌷𑌵𑌿𑌮𑍁𑌕𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌕𑌾𑌮𑍋 𑌗𑌙𑍍𑌗𑌾𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌸𑍍𑌨𑌾𑌨𑌮𑌹𑌂 𑌕𑌰𑌿𑌷𑍍𑌯𑍇, 𑌇𑌤𑌿 𑌗𑌙𑍍𑌗𑌾𑌸𑍍𑌨𑌾𑌨𑌸𑌙𑍍𑌕𑌲𑍍𑌪𑌃।  
𑌕𑍌𑌶𑌿𑌕𑍀𑌸𑍍𑌨𑌾𑌨𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌕𑌰𑌣𑍇, 𑌰𑌾𑌮𑌾𑌯𑌣𑍇 𑌆𑌦𑌿𑌕𑌾𑌣𑍍𑌡𑍇-  
𑌵𑍈𑌶𑌾𑌖𑍇 𑌮𑌾𑌸𑌿 𑌕𑌾𑌕𑍁𑌤𑍍𑌸𑍍𑌥 𑌤𑍃𑌤𑍀𑌯𑌾 𑌯𑌾 𑌭𑌵𑍇𑌤𑍍 𑌤𑌿𑌥𑌿𑌃।  
𑌶𑍁𑌕𑍍𑌲𑌪𑌕𑍍𑌷𑍇 𑌨𑌰𑌃 𑌸𑍍𑌨𑌾𑌤𑍍𑌵𑌾 𑌅𑌶𑍍𑌵𑌮𑍇𑌧𑌫𑌲𑌂 𑌲𑌭𑍇𑌤𑍍॥  
𑌕𑍃𑌤𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌕𑌾 𑌋𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌸𑌂𑌯𑍁𑌕𑍍𑌤𑌾 𑌰𑌾𑌕𑌾 𑌯𑌾 𑌕𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌕𑍇 𑌭𑌵𑍇𑌤𑍍।  
𑌕𑍋𑌕𑌾𑌮𑍁𑌖𑍇 𑌤𑍁 𑌕𑍌𑌶𑌿𑌕𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌸𑍍𑌨𑌾𑌤𑍍𑌵𑌾 𑌸𑍍𑌵𑌰𑍍𑌗𑍇 𑌵𑌸𑍇𑌨𑍍𑌨𑌰𑌃॥

4ec9fd0a03.b: Graha-yuddha (amshu-vimarda) between guruḥ and śukraḥ in maghā siṁhaḥ, center-to-center separation 0°29′38.24″.
4ec9fd0a03.d:
This is an amshu-vimarda (a collision of rays -- the discs themselves do not touch): center-to-center separation 0°29′38.24″, 0°29′18.35″ apart, disc-to-disc. guruḥ at maghā-4 siṁhaḥ (latitude 0°54′55.92″ N, Rju (direct), magnitude -1.70, elongation 3°59′28.98″ E). śukraḥ at maghā-4 siṁhaḥ (latitude 1°24′34.16″ N, Rju (direct), magnitude -3.91, elongation 4°07′58.00″ E). Classical texts weigh both the northern position and the greater apparent brightness/nearness in deciding the victor (jayI) of a yuddha; here śukraḥ is towards the north (traditionally said to prevail), while by brightness/nearness (the larger apparent diameter) guruḥ is taken as jayI over śukraḥ. A graha-yuddha (also called amshu-vimarda, "collision of rays") occurs when two of the five tArA grahas -- budha, śukra, aṅgāraka, br̥haspati, śanaiśchara -- come within 1 aMsha (60 kalA) of each other in longitude, close enough that they may be difficult to tell apart in the sky. It is called yuddha proper only when their discs actually touch/overlap; otherwise, amshu-vimarda.

The Surya Siddhanta itself cautions that this matter is described only to indicate the auspicious/inauspicious effects for people -- in reality the grahas remain far apart from one another and continue along their own paths. This is not to be received with fear, but as an advance, compassionate intimation from those who calculated these movements accurately, meant to help people take protective measures in time.

Classical texts (e.g. Brihat Samhita ch. 17) weigh both which graha is to the north and which is more prominent (nearer/brighter, of larger apparent diameter) in declaring a victor (jayī) of the yuddha; the defeated (jita) graha's significations are said to suffer for a particular section of society -- this is never a universal ill effect. The traditional response is to increase one's spiritual efforts: japa, homa, dAna and parAyaNa (especially of the Navagraha stotra), with higher AvRtti for the two grahas actually involved, particularly if the day also coincides with some other puNya kAla (e.g. a sAyana saGkramaNa).

Per the Narada Samhita (as cited in Muhurta Chintamani), the nakshatra in which a graha-yuddha occurs should be avoided for auspicious functions (vivAha, upanayana etc.) for six months following the event. If this cannot be avoided, perform parihAra for candra-bala.

Avoid food: 09:33►19:53 (from 3 yaamas before the yaama of first contact, until the eclipse's end). Pregnant women should avoid exposure to the sun/moon's light during the respective eclipse.

4f55d6be48.d:
Beginning of Dhanurmasa puja in temples and at homes. A very early morning puja is performed, typically with mudgānnam as naivedyam. Begets fruit equivalent to performing puja for a thousand years!
The two ayana-s of the Sun are night and day for the Devas. 30 of these days become a month. The uṣahkāla of their day starts in chāpamāsa i.e. dhanurmāsa (although the shloka refers to the sidereal month, it appears logical to use the tropical month, owing to its association with uttarāyaṇam). Therefore, one must strive to perform uṣahkāla-pujā in this month, before sunrise --- a ṣōḍaśōpachāra-pūjā. Following this, one must perform Sandhyavandam and upasthanam! The Shivapurana also extols the uniqueness of the early morning puja in this month, suggesting that one must perform rudrābhiṣeka.

4f79d9e60a.b: Graha-yuddha (amshu-vimarda) between aṅgārakaḥ and śukraḥ in pūrvāṣāḍhā dhanuḥ, center-to-center separation 0°10′25.60″.
4f79d9e60a.d:
This is an amshu-vimarda (a collision of rays -- the discs themselves do not touch): center-to-center separation 0°10′25.60″, 0°10′18.77″ apart, disc-to-disc. aṅgārakaḥ at pūrvāṣāḍhā-4 dhanuḥ (latitude 0°56′03.50″ S, Rju (direct), magnitude +1.08, elongation 0°59′32.61″ E). śukraḥ at pūrvāṣāḍhā-4 dhanuḥ (latitude 0°45′37.90″ S, Rju (direct), magnitude -3.91, elongation 0°49′52.32″ E). Classical texts weigh both the northern position and the greater apparent brightness/nearness in deciding the victor (jayI) of a yuddha; here aṅgārakaḥ is towards the north (traditionally said to prevail), while by brightness/nearness (the larger apparent diameter) śukraḥ is taken as jayI over aṅgārakaḥ. A graha-yuddha (also called amshu-vimarda, "collision of rays") occurs when two of the five tArA grahas -- budha, śukra, aṅgāraka, br̥haspati, śanaiśchara -- come within 1 aMsha (60 kalA) of each other in longitude, close enough that they may be difficult to tell apart in the sky. It is called yuddha proper only when their discs actually touch/overlap; otherwise, amshu-vimarda.

The Surya Siddhanta itself cautions that this matter is described only to indicate the auspicious/inauspicious effects for people -- in reality the grahas remain far apart from one another and continue along their own paths. This is not to be received with fear, but as an advance, compassionate intimation from those who calculated these movements accurately, meant to help people take protective measures in time.

Classical texts (e.g. Brihat Samhita ch. 17) weigh both which graha is to the north and which is more prominent (nearer/brighter, of larger apparent diameter) in declaring a victor (jayī) of the yuddha; the defeated (jita) graha's significations are said to suffer for a particular section of society -- this is never a universal ill effect. The traditional response is to increase one's spiritual efforts: japa, homa, dAna and parAyaNa (especially of the Navagraha stotra), with higher AvRtti for the two grahas actually involved, particularly if the day also coincides with some other puNya kAla (e.g. a sAyana saGkramaNa).

Per the Narada Samhita (as cited in Muhurta Chintamani), the nakshatra in which a graha-yuddha occurs should be avoided for auspicious functions (vivAha, upanayana etc.) for six months following the event. If this cannot be avoided, perform parihAra for candra-bala.

4f8e84dfcf.d:
The Abhidhyeyaka Abhishekam festival, also known as Jyeshthabhishekam, is a celebration held annually in the auspicious month of Jyeshtha, aligning with the Jyeshtha star in the constellation. The term “Abhidhyeyakam” refers to a protective shield or armour, symbolizing the divine defense that Bhagavan assumes in this Kaliyuga to combat evil. This festival, celebrated over three days, centers around a special abhishekam performed for this sacred armour.

According to temple traditions, this Abhishekam is conducted to safeguard the Utsava deities of Bhagavan Malayappa Swami and his consorts, Sridevi and Bhudevi. The purpose is to prevent any potential damage during various processions and holy baths (Tirumanjanam) throughout the year.

Each day of the festival, after the second bell, the deities are taken to the Kalyanotsava Mandapam situated in Sampangi Prakaram. Here, Snapana Tirumanjanam is performed, a ritual involving bathing the deities with consecrated water infused with spices, turmeric, sandal paste, honey, milk, and curd, accompanied by the chanting of Vedic mantras.

On each day, Bhagavan and his consorts are adorned in unique kavachams: The first day features the Vajrakavacham, a diamond-studded armour; the second day showcases the Muthyala kavacham, an armour studded with pearls; and the third day highlights the Svarna kavacham, a golden armour. The Svarna kavacham remains on the deities for the entire year and is only removed for the next Abhidhyeyaka Abhishekam.

It is called yuddha proper only when their discs actually touch/overlap; otherwise, amshu-vimarda.

The Surya Siddhanta itself cautions that this matter is described only to indicate the auspicious/inauspicious effects for people -- in reality the grahas remain far apart from one another and continue along their own paths. This is not to be received with fear, but as an advance, compassionate intimation from those who calculated these movements accurately, meant to help people take protective measures in time.

Classical texts (e.g. Brihat Samhita ch. 17) weigh both which graha is to the north and which is more prominent (nearer/brighter, of larger apparent diameter) in declaring a victor (jayī) of the yuddha; the defeated (jita) graha's significations are said to suffer for a particular section of society -- this is never a universal ill effect. The traditional response is to increase one's spiritual efforts: japa, homa, dAna and parAyaNa (especially of the Navagraha stotra), with higher AvRtti for the two grahas actually involved, particularly if the day also coincides with some other puNya kAla (e.g. a sAyana saGkramaNa).

Per the Narada Samhita (as cited in Muhurta Chintamani), the nakshatra in which a graha-yuddha occurs should be avoided for auspicious functions (vivAha, upanayana etc.) for six months following the event. If this cannot be avoided, perform parihAra for candra-bala.

4fcbd26044.b: Observed on Svātī nakshatra of Dhanuḥ (sidereal solar) month (Prātaḥ/paraviddha).
4fcbd26044.d:
Between the 6th and 9th centuries, in South India, there existed 63 ardent devotees of Bhagavan Shiva, collectively known as the Nayanmars. These devout individuals, hailing from various walks of life including potters, fishermen, farmers, merchants, priests, hunters, and washermen, created devotional songs still sung by followers around the globe. Among these Nayanmars, Appar, Sambandar, and Sundarar, known for their Thevaram hymns, along with Manikkavasagar, are distinguished as the Samayacharyas or the ‘The Four’ (nālvar) revered teachers of the faith. They were instrumental in promoting the Shaiva Siddhanta philosophy and culture, effectively challenging the spread of Jainism and Buddhism. Their teachings centered around the concept that Shiva embodies love, and that embracing love for all beings and existence is essential in connecting with Shiva, the Supreme Being.

In the fertile region of Kancharur within the Chola kingdom, a devout follower of Bhagavan Shiva named Manakancharanar, the 12th Nayanmar, lived. Belonging to a Vellala family and respected as a hereditary Senathipathi, he was known for his ability to intuitively serve Shiva Bhaktas without them having to ask. After a long period without children, his devout prayers were answered with the birth of a daughter, whose arrival he celebrated with extensive charity.

As the daughter grew and reached marriageable age, she was betrothed to Eyarkon Kalikamar, another sincere devotee of Bhagavan Shiva. The wedding was planned, but before it could take place, Bhagavan Shiva decided to bestow a special blessing upon Manakancharanar. Assuming the guise of a Maha-Vrathiar, a holy man with distinctive ash markings and a garland of bones, Bhagavan Shiva appeared before Manakancharanar. Inquiring about the festive preparations, the ascetic learned of the impending wedding and expressed a desire for the bride's hair to make a Panchavati, a sacred thread.

Without hesitation and disregarding the potential consequences, including the possibility of the groom rejecting his disfigured daughter, Manakancharanar cut off his daughter's hair and offered it to the ascetic. Immediately after, Bhagavan Shiva revealed his true form to Manakancharanar and his family, blessing them.

When Eyarkon Kalikamar and his party arrived and learned of the incident, they were disappointed on missing out on the darshan of Bhagavan Shiva. Further, they were dismayed to see the disfigured bride, but Bhagavan Shiva, understanding the situation, restored the daughter's hair! Relieved and overjoyed, Manakancharanar and his family proceeded with the wedding.

4ff68a1456.b: Observed on Maghā nakshatra of Siṁhaḥ (sidereal solar) month (Prātaḥ/paraviddha).
4ff68a1456.d:
Between the 6th and 9th centuries, in South India, there existed 63 ardent devotees of Bhagavan Shiva, collectively known as the Nayanmars. These devout individuals, hailing from various walks of life including potters, fishermen, farmers, merchants, priests, hunters, and washermen, created devotional songs still sung by followers around the globe. Among these Nayanmars, Appar, Sambandar, and Sundarar, known for their Thevaram hymns, along with Manikkavasagar, are distinguished as the Samayacharyas or the ‘The Four’ (nālvar) revered teachers of the faith. They were instrumental in promoting the Shaiva Siddhanta philosophy and culture, effectively challenging the spread of Jainism and Buddhism. Their teachings centered around the concept that Shiva embodies love, and that embracing love for all beings and existence is essential in connecting with Shiva, the Supreme Being.

The 4th of the Nayanmars was Ilayankudi Mara Nayanmar, a farmer named Maranar from the village of Ilayankudi. He was a devout follower of Bhagavan Shiva and His devotees. He practiced Maaheswara Puja, a form of worship involving honouring and serving Bhagavan Shiva's devotees with utmost reverence, as if serving Bhagavan Himself. This included welcoming devotees, washing their feet, offering them food, and treating them with great respect and kindness.

Though Nayanmar was blessed with wealth, he believed his riches were meant to serve Bhagavan's devotees. His devotion remained steadfast even as his wealth dwindled. Eventually, he sold all his possessions and even himself to continue serving the devotees.

One rainy day, with no food at home, Nayanmar and his wife were visited by a Shiva Bhakta. Despite their own hunger, they welcomed the devotee warmly. Nayanmar's wife suggested gathering the grain-seeds they had recently sown to prepare a meal. After they fed the devotee and Nayanmar went to check on him, he found the devotee had vanished. Instead, Bhagavan Shiva and Mother Parvathy appeared in the sky, revealing that the devotee was Bhagavan Shiva in disguise. They blessed Nayanmar and his wife for their unwavering devotion and promised them eternal life in the divine abode. This story exemplifies the profound impact of selfless service and devotion to the Supreme and His devotees.
